t: What Is “the Falling Away” in 2 Thessalonians 2:3?
s: Paul means a departure: the gathering of the Body of Christ to the Lord that he names in verse 1. The one who now hinders (verses 6–7) is the Body’s presence and ministry in the world, and when that is taken out of the way the man of sin is revealed and the day of the Lord follows.
a: The falling away is the departure of the Body of Christ, the gathering to the Lord that must take place before the day of the Lord begins. Paul is not warning believers of a coming collapse of faith. He is assuring them that they are not in the day.

t: What Was Paul’s “Thorn in the Flesh”?
s: The thorn was opposition: a messenger of Satan sent to buffet Paul in his ministry. The Lord’s answer, “My grace is sufficient for thee,” meets the pressure of that opposition, not a bodily illness.
a: The thorn was opposition: a messenger of Satan sent to buffet Paul in his ministry. It was not an illness. The Lord’s answer, “My grace is sufficient for thee,” meets that pressure, and Paul’s own list that follows is of reproaches, necessities, persecutions and distresses.

t: Is “the Last Trump” the Seventh Trumpet of Revelation?
s: No. The last trump and the trump of God belong to the Body’s gathering, a mystery Paul shows to the Corinthians. The seventh trumpet (Revelation 11:15) sounds in the Tribulation program that Revelation addresses, and Paul never mentions it.
a: No. The last trump of 1 Corinthians 15 and the trump of God of 1 Thessalonians 4 are the Body’s trumpet, sounded at a gathering Paul calls a mystery. The seventh trumpet of Revelation 11:15 sounds for the kingdoms of this world to become the Lord’s, and Paul never mentions it.

t: Is Salvation by Repentance or by Belief?
s: The Body is saved by believing the gospel Paul preached, through grace and not of works. Repentance is a change of mind that accompanies believing; the passages that command it do so in their own settings and never as a second ground of salvation.
a: The Body is saved by believing the gospel Paul preached, by grace through faith and not of works. Repentance is the change of mind that goes with believing. The passages that command it are each addressed in their own setting, and none of them adds a second ground to the gospel of grace.

t: Why Were Sodom and Gomorrah Destroyed?
s: Scripture names more than one sin, and none is left out. Genesis gives a great cry and a grievous sin, climaxing in the mob at Lot’s door; Ezekiel names pride, fulness of bread, idleness and neglect of the poor; Jude names fornication and going after strange flesh.
a: Scripture names more than one sin, and none is left out. Genesis gives a great cry and a grievous sin, and the city’s men at Lot’s door; Ezekiel gives pride, fulness of bread, idleness and neglect of the poor; Jude gives fornication and going after strange flesh. The judgment is the Lord’s, and the sins belong together.

t: Does Romans 10:9–10 Make Confession a Condition of the Body’s Salvation?
s: No. Romans 10 is addressed to Israel, and verse 9 is Israel’s covenantal salvation formula, drawn from Deuteronomy 30. Confession is Israel’s covenantal expression and has no saving function for the Body, which is saved by belief alone in the gospel Paul preached (1 Corinthians 15:1–4; Ephesians 2:8–9).
a: No, because Romans 10 is not addressed to the Body. It sits inside Romans 9–11, Paul’s address to Israel, and verse 9 is Israel’s covenantal salvation formula, drawn from Deuteronomy 30. Confession belongs to that formula and is Israel’s covenantal expression. It has no saving function for the Body, which is saved by belief alone in the gospel Paul preached (1 Corinthians 15:1–4; Ephesians 2:8–9).

t: What Does It Mean to “Grieve Not the Holy Spirit of God”?
s: It is a command about conduct. The sins around it in the passage (lying, unrestrained wrath, corrupt speech, bitterness) hurt the Spirit who dwells in the believer, yet the same verse says the believer is “sealed unto the day of redemption,” so grieving affects fellowship and not security.
a: It is a command about conduct. The sins around it (lying, wrath that gives the devil a place, corrupt speech, bitterness) grieve the Spirit who dwells in the believer, yet the same verse says the believer is “sealed unto the day of redemption.” Grieving affects fellowship and the believer’s walk, not the security of the seal.

t: To Whom Are the Words “Well Done, Thou Good and Faithful Servant” Spoken?
s: They are the King’s words to faithful servants in Israel’s kingdom, in a parable given on the Mount of Olives. The reward is rule “over many things” and entering “the joy of thy lord”; the passage is not the Body’s judgment seat.
a: They are the King’s words to faithful servants in Israel’s kingdom, in a parable given on the Mount of Olives. The reward is rule “over many things” and entering “the joy of thy lord.” The passage is not the Body’s judgment seat.

t: What Does “The Kingdom of Heaven Suffereth Violence” Mean?
s: The kingdom has been assaulted since John’s days. John is in prison when the saying is spoken, and the violent who “take it by force” are its opponents, not eager seekers pressing in.
a: The kingdom has been assaulted since the days of John. John is in prison when the saying is spoken, and “the violent” who “take it by force” are its opponents. The saying is about the kingdom’s resistance, not about eager seekers pressing in.

t: Is the “Everlasting Father” of Isaiah 9:6 God the Father?
s: The title belongs to the child born, who sits on David’s throne (9:7). It names him as a father to his people who does not die, a role Scripture also gives to a faithful steward, “a father to the inhabitants of Jerusalem” (22:21), and does not confuse the Son with the Father.
a: The title belongs to the child born, who sits on David’s throne. It names him as a father to his people who does not die, a role Isaiah himself gives to a faithful steward, “a father to the inhabitants of Jerusalem.” It does not say the Son is the Father.

t: Who Is “Taken” and Who Is “Left” in Matthew 24:40–41?
s: The one “taken” is taken away in judgment, as the flood “took them all away,” and the one “left” remains to enter the kingdom. The passage is Israel’s separation at the Lord’s coming, spoken to disciples on the Mount of Olives. It is not the gathering of the Body.
a: The one “taken” is taken away in judgment, as the flood “took them all away,” and the one “left” remains to enter the kingdom. The passage is Israel’s separation at the Lord’s coming, spoken to disciples on the Mount of Olives. It is not the gathering of the Body.

t: Who Is “the Israel of God” in Galatians 6:16?
s: “The Israel of God” is believing Israel: the prophetic remnant of ethnic Jews who have embraced Messiah and remain members of Israel’s Prophecy Program, within Israel’s prophetic identity, named beside the Body and not as the Body. They are not absorbed into the Body, and their identity, destiny and program membership stay intact.
a: “The Israel of God” is believing Israel: the prophetic remnant of ethnic Jews who have embraced Messiah and remain members of Israel’s Prophecy Program, within Israel’s prophetic identity, named beside the Body and not as the Body. They are not absorbed into the Body, and their identity, destiny and program membership stay intact. Paul gives peace to “as many as walk according to this rule,” and mercy also “upon the Israel of God.” The phrase is a benediction on Jewish believers who walk by the rule just stated. The Body is not Israel, and Israel is not the Body.

t: Is the Great Commission Given to the Body of Christ?
s: The commission of Matthew 28:18–20 was spoken to the eleven on a mountain in Galilee, after Matthew 10 sent them to “the lost sheep of the house of Israel.” It widens the field to the nations and ties the work to the kingdom commands and “the end of the world.” The Body’s commission is Paul’s, the ministry of reconciliation, and Paul says Christ “sent me not to baptize.”
a: The commission of Matthew 28:18–20 was spoken to the eleven on a mountain in Galilee, after Matthew 10 sent them to “the lost sheep of the house of Israel.” It widens the field to the nations and ties the work to the kingdom commands and “the end of the world.” The Body’s commission is Paul’s, the ministry of reconciliation, and Paul says Christ “sent me not to baptize.”

t: Is Water Baptism Required for the Body’s Salvation?
s: No. The Body is saved by grace through faith, and its one baptism is the work of the Spirit, “by one Spirit are we all baptized into one body.” The passages that join water to salvation are spoken in Israel’s setting, where baptism attends the kingdom message.
a: No. The Body is saved by grace through faith, and its one baptism is the work of the Spirit, “by one Spirit are we all baptized into one body.” The passages that join water to salvation are spoken in Israel’s setting, where baptism attends the kingdom message. Even there the sentence that condemns names unbelief and not an unbaptized state.

t: Can a Believer Lose Salvation According to Hebrews 6:4–6?
s: No, because the passage is not a warning to the Body. Hebrews is written to Israel, and the warning is Israel’s danger of rejecting the Messiah after receiving the kingdom’s signs (“the powers of the world to come”), which is to crucify the Son afresh. The Body’s security rests on promises the passage never touches: “neither death, nor life … shall be able to separate us.”
a: No, because the passage is not a warning to the Body. Hebrews is written to Israel, and the warning is Israel’s danger of rejecting the Messiah after receiving the kingdom’s signs (“the powers of the world to come”), which is to crucify the Son afresh. The Body’s security rests on promises the passage never touches: “neither death, nor life … shall be able to separate us.”

t: Who Is the Male Child of Revelation 12:5?
s: The male child is the company of the 144,000, Israel’s firstfruits remnant, and not the person of Christ. The child is “caught up unto God,” a word of removal used of those taken up, and the same company reappears with the Lamb on mount Sion in Revelation 14:1–5 as “firstfruits.” The rod of iron is shared with overcomers in Revelation 2:26–27.
a: The male child is the company of the 144,000, Israel’s firstfruits remnant, and not the person of Christ. The child is “caught up unto God,” a word of removal used of those taken up, and the same company reappears with the Lamb on mount Sion in Revelation 14:1–5 as “firstfruits.” The rod of iron is shared with overcomers in Revelation 2:26–27.

t: Who Is “All Israel” in Romans 11:26?
s: “All Israel” is the nation of Israel, saved at the coming of the Deliverer, after “the fulness of the Gentiles” has come in. It is not the Body, not “spiritual Israel” and not the whole company of the elect from every nation. Romans 9–11 is spoken to Israel and concerns Israel.
a: “All Israel” is the nation of Israel, saved at the coming of the Deliverer, after “the fulness of the Gentiles” has come in. It is not the Body, not “spiritual Israel” and not the whole company of the elect from every nation. Romans 9–11 is spoken to Israel and concerns Israel.

t: What Is the Unpardonable Sin?
s: It is the blasphemy against the Holy Ghost spoken in Matthew 12: the leaders’ ascribing the King’s works, done by the Spirit of God, to Beelzebub. It was said of Israel’s generation in the presence of the King, and the sentence reaches “neither in this world, neither in the world to come.”
a: It is the blasphemy against the Holy Ghost spoken in Matthew 12: the leaders’ ascribing the King’s works, done by the Spirit of God, to Beelzebub. It was said of Israel’s generation in the presence of the King, and the sentence reaches “neither in this world, neither in the world to come.” The Body cannot commit it: Paul never warns the Body of any such sin, and the Body is “sealed” by the Spirit and told it is “forgiven … all trespasses.”

t: Who Are “the Sons of God” in Genesis 6:1–4?
s: The sons of God are angelic beings. The same title is used of them in Job 1:6 and 38:7, and Peter and Jude set angels who sinned beside the flood and Sodom. The Lord’s words in Matthew 22:30 describe people in the resurrection and do not decide what angels could do before.
a: The sons of God are angelic beings. The same title is used of them in Job 1:6 and 38:7, and Peter and Jude set angels who sinned beside the flood and Sodom. The Lord’s words in Matthew 22:30 describe people in the resurrection and do not decide what angels could do before.

t: What Does “Baptized for the Dead” Mean in 1 Corinthians 15:29?
s: It names a practice of some at Corinth, spoken of as “they,” and Paul uses it as an argument without commending it or commanding it. The passage is part of his proof that the dead rise. The Body has no ordinance of baptism on behalf of the dead.
a: It names a practice of some at Corinth, spoken of as “they,” and Paul uses it as an argument without commending it or commanding it. The passage is part of his proof that the dead rise. The Body has no ordinance of baptism on behalf of the dead.

t: What Does “Take Up His Cross, and Follow Me” Mean in Matthew 16:24?
s: This is Kingdom-discipleship instruction, spoken by Christ in his earthly ministry to Israel’s disciples. “Take up his cross” is the figure of a condemned man: self-denial, readiness to suffer and loyalty to the Messiah as they follow him toward the promised kingdom, with the reward when the Son of man comes “in his kingdom.”
a: This is Kingdom-discipleship instruction, spoken by Christ in his earthly ministry to Israel’s disciples. “Take up his cross” is the figure of a condemned man: self-denial, readiness to suffer and loyalty to the Messiah as they follow him toward the promised kingdom, with the reward when the Son of man comes “in his kingdom.” It is the requirement for Israel’s remnant and it is not a command to the Body of Christ, which is never told to take up a cross or to follow Jesus on his earthly path. The Body’s word is that it is “crucified with Christ.”

t: What Does “Out of Egypt Have I Called My Son” Mean in Hosea 11:1 and Matthew 2:15?
s: Hosea 11:1 looks back. It is the Lord’s own word that Israel, his covenant son, was called out of Egypt at the exodus. Matthew applies the same line to Jesus, God’s eternal Son, whose flight into Egypt and return re-live Israel’s pattern.
a: Hosea 11:1 looks back. It is the Lord’s own word that Israel, his covenant son, was called out of Egypt at the exodus. Matthew applies the same line to Jesus, God’s eternal Son, whose flight into Egypt and return re-live Israel’s pattern. These are two sons, each in his own place: Israel in national sonship, Christ in his own Sonship. Matthew’s use is typological fulfilment, not a transfer of identity: Israel remains Israel, and Jesus does not replace Israel. He does not claim that Hosea was predicting the infant’s journey.

t: What Does “Quench Not the Spirit” Mean in 1 Thessalonians 5:19?
s: The command is given to the Body of Christ. To quench the Spirit is to stifle or hinder his present-age ministry in the believer: his teaching, his work of growth and his work of sanctification. The Body quenches him by resisting his teaching through Paul’s doctrine, by rejecting truth, or by persisting in the flesh.
a: The command is given to the Body of Christ. To quench the Spirit is to stifle or hinder his present-age ministry in the believer: his teaching, his work of growth and his work of sanctification. The Body quenches him by resisting his teaching through Paul’s doctrine, by rejecting truth, or by persisting in the flesh. It is a warning against stagnation. It is not about losing salvation or losing the Spirit, since God “hath also given unto us his holy Spirit,” and it is a different command from “grieve not the holy Spirit” in Ephesians 4:30.

t: What Does “Work Out Your Own Salvation with Fear and Trembling” Mean in Philippians 2:12?
s: It is a word to the Body about living out the salvation it already has, and it is not about earning or keeping it. “Work out” means to bring to full expression what God has already worked within; the matter is sanctification, not justification.
a: It is a word to the Body about living out the salvation it already has, and it is not about earning or keeping it. “Work out” means to bring to full expression what God has already worked within; the matter is sanctification, not justification. “Fear and trembling” is seriousness, humility and dependence on God’s enabling, and the very next verse says so: “it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure.” It is instruction for the Body’s spiritual maturity and is not Kingdom-discipleship language.

t: What Does “Deliver Such an One unto Satan” Mean in 1 Corinthians 5:5?
s: This is the Body’s own discipline. Paul tells the assembly at Corinth, gathered with his spirit and the power of the Lord, to remove a brother who persists in open immorality from its fellowship, putting him outside the protective sphere of the gathered assembly and so out into the world where Satan holds sway, “for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus.”
a: This is the Body’s own discipline. Paul tells the assembly at Corinth, gathered with his spirit and the power of the Lord, to remove a brother who persists in open immorality from its fellowship, putting him outside the protective sphere of the gathered assembly and so out into the world where Satan holds sway, “for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus.” The “destruction of the flesh” is disciplinary affliction, physical or circumstantial, that God permits when the man is removed from the assembly’s protection, aimed at breaking the sinful pattern. The man is a brother, the purpose is corrective and aimed at restoring him, and the second letter shows him grieved and received back. It is corrective and not punitive: not a curse, not annihilation, not the loss of salvation and not Israel’s covenant penalty.

t: Who Are “the Spirits in Prison” in 1 Peter 3:19?
s: They are angelic beings and not human souls: the angels who sinned in the days of Noah, now held in prison for judgment (2 Peter 2:4; Jude 6). After he was “quickened by the Spirit,” Christ made a proclamation to them.
a: They are angelic beings and not human souls: the angels who sinned in the days of Noah, now held in prison for judgment (2 Peter 2:4; Jude 6). After he was “quickened by the Spirit,” Christ made a proclamation to them. The word is the herald’s word, a declaration of his victory and of their judgment, and it is not an offer of the gospel to the dead. The passage ends with “angels and authorities and powers being made subject unto him.” It is written to Israel’s scattered believers and has no connection with the Body’s heavenly calling.

t: What Is “the Sin unto Death” in 1 John 5:16?
s: It is physical death, not the loss of salvation, which God brings on a believer who persists in severe, unrepentant sin. It is a discipline of God and not a covenant curse: God takes the believer from earthly life to prevent further damage to his testimony, as in the Corinthians among whom “many are weak and sickly,” and “many sleep.”
a: It is physical death, not the loss of salvation, which God brings on a believer who persists in severe, unrepentant sin. It is a discipline of God and not a covenant curse: God takes the believer from earthly life to prevent further damage to his testimony, as in the Corinthians among whom “many are weak and sickly,” and “many sleep.” It is not eternal death, damnation or the loss of eternal life, and the passage is set in a letter written “that ye may know that ye have eternal life.” The apostle does not name the sin and does not forbid praying for such a brother. It is not the unpardonable sin of Matthew 12.

t: What Does “The Just Shall Live by His Faith” Mean in Habakkuk 2:4?
s: The sentence has two program-specific applications that never merge. In Habakkuk, in Israel’s program, it is God’s answer to a prophet who cannot see how he can use a cruel nation to judge his own people: the proud man’s “soul … is not upright in him,” but Israel’s faithful remnant will keep its life through the coming national distress by trusting God’s promises, “though it tarry, wait for it.”
a: The sentence has two program-specific applications that never merge. In Habakkuk, in Israel’s program, it is God’s answer to a prophet who cannot see how he can use a cruel nation to judge his own people: the proud man’s “soul … is not upright in him,” but Israel’s faithful remnant will keep its life through the coming national distress by trusting God’s promises, “though it tarry, wait for it.” In the Mystery, Paul takes the same sentence to teach that the saints of the Body live by faith apart from the Law (Romans 1:17; Galatians 3:11). The writer to the Hebrews uses it within Israel’s line, to call suffering believers to endure. It states a universal truth, and it works differently in each program’s own structure.

t: Who Are “the Meek” Who “Inherit the Earth” in Matthew 5:5?
s: This is Kingdom prophecy, spoken by Christ to Israel. The meek are Israel’s faithful remnant, those who wait on the Lord and leave vengeance to him, as Psalm 37 says in the very words the Lord uses: “the meek shall inherit the earth.” They are the ones who will enter and inherit the earthly kingdom of the Messiah.
a: This is Kingdom prophecy, spoken by Christ to Israel. The meek are Israel’s faithful remnant, those who wait on the Lord and leave vengeance to him, as Psalm 37 says in the very words the Lord uses: “the meek shall inherit the earth.” They are the ones who will enter and inherit the earthly kingdom of the Messiah. The Body of Christ does not inherit the earth: its destiny is “in heavenly places.” The promise belongs to Israel’s covenant hope and is not transferred to the Body.

t: What Does “The Kingdom of God Is within You” Mean in Luke 17:21?
s: Jesus is speaking to Israel during his earthly ministry, to Pharisees who were asking when the kingdom would come, and he answers that it does not come with signs to be watched for, because the King himself stands “in the midst of” them. The words cannot mean that the kingdom was inside those men, who were rejecting him. It is a statement about the nearness of Israel’s promised kingdom, because the King was physically present.
a: Jesus is speaking to Israel during his earthly ministry, to Pharisees who were asking when the kingdom would come, and he answers that it does not come with signs to be watched for, because the King himself stands “in the midst of” them. The words cannot mean that the kingdom was inside those men, who were rejecting him. It is a statement about the nearness of Israel’s promised kingdom, because the King was physically present. The visible kingdom in power is still ahead: he turns to his disciples and speaks of “the day when the Son of man is revealed.” It is not the Body’s heavenly kingdom and not an internal reign.

t: What Does “He That Endureth to the End Shall Be Saved” Mean in Matthew 10:22 and 24:13?
s: It is a promise to Israel’s remnant in the Tribulation: the one who holds out to the end of those days will be brought through alive. “The end” is the end of the Tribulation, when the Son of man comes, and not the end of a person’s life; “saved” is physical deliverance through the persecution and the deceptions of that time, and not eternal salvation.
a: It is a promise to Israel’s remnant in the Tribulation: the one who holds out to the end of those days will be brought through alive. “The end” is the end of the Tribulation, when the Son of man comes, and not the end of a person’s life; “saved” is physical deliverance through the persecution and the deceptions of that time, and not eternal salvation. The Lord says it first to the Twelve, sent “to the lost sheep of the house of Israel,” and again on the mount of Olives in answer to a question about “the end of the world.” Endurance here is survival, not merit, and eternal salvation is never made to hang on endurance in any program. The saying was not spoken to the Body, which is not in the Tribulation and is not under kingdom requirements; its salvation rests on believing the gospel Paul preached (1 Corinthians 15:1–4).

t: What Does “Faith without Works Is Dead” Mean in James 2:26?
s: It means that a faith which is only a claim, with nothing done, is lifeless and useless, as a body without breath is lifeless. James writes to “the twelve tribes which are scattered abroad,” Israel’s prophetic remnant, and his examples, Abraham and Rahab, are figures of Israel’s covenant story.
a: It means that a faith which is only a claim, with nothing done, is lifeless and useless, as a body without breath is lifeless. James writes to “the twelve tribes which are scattered abroad,” Israel’s prophetic remnant, and his examples, Abraham and Rahab, are figures of Israel’s covenant story. In that setting faith is expected to express itself in covenant obedience, and works are what show the faith is alive: “I will shew thee my faith by my works.” Works do not save; they demonstrate living faith. This is not Paul’s teaching on justification, which is salvation by grace through faith alone for the Body. James addresses faithfulness within Israel’s prophetic identity, and the Body’s works relate to reward and not to justification (1 Corinthians 3:11–15).

t: What Does “Baptism Doth Also Now Save Us” Mean in 1 Peter 3:21?
s: Peter writes to Israel’s scattered believers, and water baptism belongs to Israel’s covenant response in the kingdom offer and the early part of Acts (“Repent, and be baptized,” Acts 2:38). He calls baptism the answering figure to the ark: as eight souls were brought through the flood by water, so baptism now “saves” in a figure, and he guards the point at once.
a: Peter writes to Israel’s scattered believers, and water baptism belongs to Israel’s covenant response in the kingdom offer and the early part of Acts (“Repent, and be baptized,” Acts 2:38). He calls baptism the answering figure to the ark: as eight souls were brought through the flood by water, so baptism now “saves” in a figure, and he guards the point at once. “Saves” here is deliverance from the judgment that hung over Israel in that prophetic setting, not eternal salvation; and it is “not the putting away of the filth of the flesh,” but “the answer of a good conscience toward God,” which in Israel’s setting is a covenant loyalty, with the saving “by the resurrection of Jesus Christ.” It is not the Body’s baptism, the one baptism of Ephesians 4:5 and the Spirit’s baptism into the one body (1 Corinthians 12:13). Paul says Christ sent him “not to baptize, but to preach the gospel” (1 Corinthians 1:17), which shows water baptism is no part of the saving message of the Body.

t: What Does “Call upon the Name of the Lord” Mean in Romans 10:13?
s: It is Israel’s own way of seeking the Lord’s deliverance. Paul quotes the line from Joel 2:32, where “whosoever shall call on the name of the Lord shall be delivered” belongs to the day of the Lord, to “mount Zion and in Jerusalem” and to “the remnant whom the Lord shall call.”
a: It is Israel’s own way of seeking the Lord’s deliverance. Paul quotes the line from Joel 2:32, where “whosoever shall call on the name of the Lord shall be delivered” belongs to the day of the Lord, to “mount Zion and in Jerusalem” and to “the remnant whom the Lord shall call.” Romans 9–11 is addressed to Israel and concerns Israel, and Paul’s point at 10:12–13 is that the Lord is “the same Lord over all” and that no difference is made between the Jew and the Greek who call on him. The phrase is Israel’s covenantal cry for deliverance; for the Body it is not a sinner’s prayer and not the way of being saved. Calling expresses faith and is not the mechanism of salvation. The Body is saved by believing the gospel Paul preached (1 Corinthians 15:1–4), and what Paul says of the Body’s salvation is in Ephesians 2:8–9.

t: What Does “Judge Not” Mean in Matthew 7:1?
s: The Lord forbids the censorious, self-exempting judging of a brother, the kind that sees “the mote” in another’s eye and will not look at “the beam” in one’s own, and he warns that the measure used will come back on the one who uses it. He does not forbid discernment.
a: The Lord forbids the censorious, self-exempting judging of a brother, the kind that sees “the mote” in another’s eye and will not look at “the beam” in one’s own, and he warns that the measure used will come back on the one who uses it. He does not forbid discernment. In the same passage he commands his hearers to “Give not that which is holy unto the dogs” and to know false prophets “by their fruits,” which cannot be done without judging. The saying is part of the Sermon on the Mount, given to his disciples in Israel’s kingdom ministry. The Body has its own words on judging, and they show the saying is not universal: Paul tells it to judge matters within the assembly (1 Corinthians 5:12; 6:1–5) and not to judge a brother over disputable things (Romans 14). They are not this saying carried over.

t: What Does “Until Seventy Times Seven” Mean in Matthew 18:22?
s: It means that there is no number at which forgiveness stops; the number is symbolic of limitless forgiveness, as God is patient with Israel. Peter asks how often he must forgive a brother who sins against him, and offers “till seven times?”, a generous count; the Lord answers, “Until seventy times seven,” and tells the parable of the servant who was forgiven ten thousand talents and would not forgive a hundred pence.
a: It means that there is no number at which forgiveness stops; the number is symbolic of limitless forgiveness, as God is patient with Israel. Peter asks how often he must forgive a brother who sins against him, and offers “till seven times?”, a generous count; the Lord answers, “Until seventy times seven,” and tells the parable of the servant who was forgiven ten thousand talents and would not forgive a hundred pence. The saying is given to Israel’s disciples in the kingdom ministry, where the Father’s forgiveness is shown answering the disciple’s own and ends with a warning, “if ye from your hearts forgive not.” Forgiveness is also taught in Paul’s letters, but this is not a Body command. The Body is told to forgive “even as God for Christ’s sake hath forgiven you,” which begins from forgiveness already given and carries no such warning.

t: What Does “Sell All That Thou Hast” Mean in Luke 18:22?
s: It is the Lord’s own test of one man, a command to an individual and not a universal rule, a ruler who asked what he must do to inherit eternal life, and it is part of the kingdom discipleship he set before Israel. The ruler said he had kept the commandments from his youth.
a: It is the Lord’s own test of one man, a command to an individual and not a universal rule, a ruler who asked what he must do to inherit eternal life, and it is part of the kingdom discipleship he set before Israel. The ruler said he had kept the commandments from his youth. The Lord answered, “Yet lackest thou one thing: sell all that thou hast, and distribute unto the poor,” and the man went away “very sorrowful: for he was very rich.” The command exposed what ruled him. It is not a rule that the Body must sell its possessions; the Twelve’s company in Acts 2–4 shared what it had in expectation of the kingdom, and Paul never commands the Body to sell all. Paul tells the Body’s rich to be “ready to distribute,” which is a different instruction, and nothing in the saying makes poverty the price of salvation.

t: What Does “The Last Shall Be First” Mean in Matthew 19:30 and 20:16?
s: It is a saying about reward in the kingdom, and it warns those who count their service that God’s gift is his own to give. Peter has just asked, “what shall we have therefore?”, and the Lord promises the Twelve thrones “judging the twelve tribes of Israel” and a hundredfold to all who have left their all.
a: It is a saying about reward in the kingdom, and it warns those who count their service that God’s gift is his own to give. Peter has just asked, “what shall we have therefore?”, and the Lord promises the Twelve thrones “judging the twelve tribes of Israel” and a hundredfold to all who have left their all. Then he says “many that are first shall be last; and the last shall be first,” and tells the parable of the householder who paid every labourer a penny, and closes with the saying again. The first must not presume on their place, and the last may be given what the first received. The householder’s answer, “Is it not lawful for me to do what I will with mine own?”, is the point. It concerns reward in Israel’s kingdom and not the Body’s.

t: What Does “My Yoke Is Easy” Mean in Matthew 11:30?
s: It is the Lord’s invitation to Israel’s weary to take his teaching in place of the burden that the scribes and Pharisees laid on them. “Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me.”
a: It is the Lord’s invitation to Israel’s weary to take his teaching in place of the burden that the scribes and Pharisees laid on them. “Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me.” A yoke is the discipleship of a pupil to his master, and the Lord’s yoke is “easy,” kind or good, because he is “meek and lowly in heart” and his burden is “light” beside the heavy burdens of the Pharisees (23:4). It is still a yoke and still asks him to be followed. It was spoken to Israel in the kingdom ministry and is not the Body’s call to be saved.

t: What Does “We Shall Judge Angels” Mean in 1 Corinthians 6:3?
s: Paul is speaking to the Body of Christ, and “judge” here means to govern and administer, not to condemn. The Body inherits the heavenly places (Ephesians 2:6) and one day fills seats of authority in them that angelic rulers held, so that our “judging” angels is taking up their governing positions, an administrative judging, as the Twelve “judge” the twelve tribes by ruling them in the earthly kingdom. It is not punitive.
a: Paul is speaking to the Body of Christ, and “judge” here means to govern and administer, not to condemn. The Body inherits the heavenly places (Ephesians 2:6) and one day fills seats of authority in them that angelic rulers held, so that our “judging” angels is taking up their governing positions, an administrative judging, as the Twelve “judge” the twelve tribes by ruling them in the earthly kingdom. It is not punitive. Condemning judgment belongs to Christ, the Body never takes part in the great white throne, and the casting out of angels is Michael’s work in Revelation 12, not the Body’s. Paul’s argument is from the greater to the lesser: if the Body is to govern the heavenly realm, it is fit to settle disputes on earth. This is a destiny of the Mystery, not a promise of Israel’s prophetic program, and it never involves sentencing.

t: How Do I Know God’s Will? Romans 12:2
s: The Body of Christ knows God’s will through Paul’s revelation, not through signs, dreams or prophetic guidance. Paul says the way is a renewed mind: “be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind, that ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God.”
a: The Body of Christ knows God’s will through Paul’s revelation, not through signs, dreams or prophetic guidance. Paul says the way is a renewed mind: “be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind, that ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God.” The will he then names is stated in his letters: sanctification, thanksgiving, and being “filled with the knowledge of his will in all wisdom and spiritual understanding.” The Spirit guides by opening what has been revealed, not by outward signs. The methods of Israel’s prophetic setting, such as casting lots and waiting for a voice, are not set before the Body. Wisdom comes by applying Paul’s doctrine with prayer, and the aim of the will is “Christ be formed in you.”

t: Why Does God Allow Suffering? Romans 5:3–4
s: For the Body, suffering is not covenant punishment, because the Body is not under the Law. Paul says “tribulation worketh patience; And patience, experience; and experience, hope,” and that to believe is also “to suffer for his sake.” God uses suffering to show Christ’s strength in weakness: “my strength is made perfect in weakness.”
a: For the Body, suffering is not covenant punishment, because the Body is not under the Law. Paul says “tribulation worketh patience; And patience, experience; and experience, hope,” and that to believe is also “to suffer for his sake.” God uses suffering to show Christ’s strength in weakness: “my strength is made perfect in weakness.” The Body is not promised earthly deliverance; “all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution.” Suffering loosens the hold of the world and fixes the mind on things above, and God works it with everything else “for good to them that love God.” The “light affliction” of the present “worketh for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory.” This is the Body’s word on suffering; it is not Israel’s, whose remnant is promised deliverance in the kingdom.

t: How Do I Deal with Doubt? Ephesians 1:13 and 2 Timothy 3:15
s: Doubt is met by returning to what Paul wrote, which steadies the mind, and the Body is not asked to look for signs to confirm it. Believers were “sealed with that holy Spirit of promise” when they believed, so doubt is not a sign of lost salvation. The Spirit helps by opening what God has given, “that we might know the things that are freely given to us of God.”
a: Doubt is met by returning to what Paul wrote, which steadies the mind, and the Body is not asked to look for signs to confirm it. Believers were “sealed with that holy Spirit of promise” when they believed, so doubt is not a sign of lost salvation. The Spirit helps by opening what God has given, “that we might know the things that are freely given to us of God.” The Lord’s refusal of a sign to Israel (“An evil and adulterous generation seeketh after a sign”) shows that asking for confirmations belongs to Israel’s setting. Doubt weakens as Scripture is read and believed, and Paul tells believers to “stand fast in the faith,” to pray with thanksgiving and to handle the word of truth rightly. Faith grows by hearing.

t: How Do I Deal with Temptation? 1 Corinthians 10:13
s: Temptation is resisted by walking in the Spirit. The Body is not under the Law, so victory does not come through legalism. Paul tells believers to “reckon ye also yourselves to be dead indeed unto sin, but alive unto God,” and promises that God “will with the temptation also make a way to escape.”
a: Temptation is resisted by walking in the Spirit. The Body is not under the Law, so victory does not come through legalism. Paul tells believers to “reckon ye also yourselves to be dead indeed unto sin, but alive unto God,” and promises that God “will with the temptation also make a way to escape.” Renewing the mind with Paul’s doctrine weakens temptation’s hold, the Spirit’s fruit includes “temperance,” and Timothy is told to “flee also youthful lusts.” Victory is rooted in who the believer is in Christ, not in willpower: “ye are dead, and your life is hid with Christ in God.”

t: How Do I Deal with Unanswered Prayer? 2 Corinthians 12:8–9
s: Unanswered prayer is not a covenant judgment on the Body, which is not under the Law and not Israel. God answers according to his wisdom, and Paul’s own case shows what that can mean: he besought the Lord three times that the thorn “might depart from me,” and the answer was “My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness.”
a: Unanswered prayer is not a covenant judgment on the Body, which is not under the Law and not Israel. God answers according to his wisdom, and Paul’s own case shows what that can mean: he besought the Lord three times that the thorn “might depart from me,” and the answer was “My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness.” Some requests are not granted because they cut across God’s purposes for the believer’s growth, and “all things work together for good to them that love God.” The Spirit helps in prayer according to the will of God and not ours. Believers are told to give thanks in everything, to continue in prayer, and to rest in the character of the God they know: “I know whom I have believed.”

t: How Do I Deal with Spiritual Dryness? Colossians 3:16
s: Dryness often comes from neglecting Scripture, prayer or fellowship, and renewal comes through Paul’s doctrine opened by the Spirit. The Body is not told to seek revival through signs or emotional experience: “we walk by faith, not by sight.” The word is the remedy: “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly.”
a: Dryness often comes from neglecting Scripture, prayer or fellowship, and renewal comes through Paul’s doctrine opened by the Spirit. The Body is not told to seek revival through signs or emotional experience: “we walk by faith, not by sight.” The word is the remedy: “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly.” Prayer turns the heart toward God, and fellowship with mature believers strengthens faith, as Paul wrote to Rome, that “I may be comforted together with you by the mutual faith both of you and me.” Dry seasons end when the believer keeps at the truth and the discipline: “let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap.” God uses them to teach dependence, as Paul learned in affliction.

t: How Do I Deal with Guilt? Colossians 2:13–14
s: Guilt is dealt with by believing that the Body is fully forgiven in Christ. Paul says God has “forgiven you all trespasses” and the “handwriting of ordinances that was against us” is gone. “Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God.”
a: Guilt is dealt with by believing that the Body is fully forgiven in Christ. Paul says God has “forgiven you all trespasses” and the “handwriting of ordinances that was against us” is gone. “Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God.” Confession acknowledges the sin, but cleansing rests on Christ’s finished work: “we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins.” Lasting guilt often comes from not understanding grace, as when the Galatians began in the Spirit and fell back on the flesh. The Spirit assures the believer of his standing: “The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God.” Guilt should lead to a change of mind, not despair, and truth, not emotion, defeats it.

t: How Do I Deal with Fear? 2 Timothy 1:7
s: Fear is met by grounding the heart in what God has given the Body. Paul says “God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind,” and that believers have not received “the spirit of bondage again to fear.” The Body is not appointed to wrath: “God hath not appointed us to wrath, but to obtain salvation.”
a: Fear is met by grounding the heart in what God has given the Body. Paul says “God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind,” and that believers have not received “the spirit of bondage again to fear.” The Body is not appointed to wrath: “God hath not appointed us to wrath, but to obtain salvation.” God’s peace “shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus” when truth is believed, and the Spirit strengthens courage as the mind is renewed. Meditation on Scripture and fellowship with other believers steady the heart. Fear is a call to deeper trust, as David wrote: “What time I am afraid, I will trust in thee,” a general truth that Paul’s teaching confirms.

t: What Is the Fate of Infants Who Die? 2 Samuel 12:23
s: Infants who die are safe with God. They have not reached the understanding by which a person is held accountable, so the Law does not condemn them, conscience has not charged them and they have not rejected a gospel. David’s word over his dead child, “I shall go to him, but he shall not return to me,” shows that God receives one who had no moral capacity.
a: Infants who die are safe with God. They have not reached the understanding by which a person is held accountable, so the Law does not condemn them, conscience has not charged them and they have not rejected a gospel. David’s word over his dead child, “I shall go to him, but he shall not return to me,” shows that God receives one who had no moral capacity. God’s justice and mercy guarantee it: “Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right?” The Body is not formed by death, because Body membership is by believing Paul’s gospel and being sealed, which an infant has not done. The infant’s end follows God’s righteousness and not speculation, and his character, “merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and plenteous in mercy,” stands behind the confidence. Their fate is mercy, not judgment.

t: What Is the Conscience? Romans 2:15
s: The conscience is the inward moral witness God put in every person. Paul says it bears witness, “their thoughts the mean while accusing or else excusing one another.” It is not infallible: some have a weak conscience that is easily wounded and “defiled.”
a: The conscience is the inward moral witness God put in every person. Paul says it bears witness, “their thoughts the mean while accusing or else excusing one another.” It is not infallible: some have a weak conscience that is easily wounded and “defiled.” It must be shaped by Scripture, especially Paul’s doctrine, and Paul allows believers to be “fully persuaded in his own mind” in matters of conscience. A strong conscience is formed by truth, as those “who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil,” a general principle. The conscience does not save but shows a person’s moral accountability: God will judge “the secrets of men by Jesus Christ according to my gospel.” The Spirit uses Scripture to renew the mind and refine the conscience. It belongs to every human, as God’s moral design for all.

t: Why Did Jesus Cry “My God, My God, Why Hast Thou Forsaken Me?” Matthew 27:46 & Psalm 22:1
s: Jesus speaks the first line of Psalm 22 at the end of the darkness, and the forsaking is real in the hour of the cross. Matthew has already built the scene from Psalm 22 before the cry. The psalm itself turns from abandonment to being heard, and Hebrews places its praise in His mouth. The Gospels do not explain the forsaking; Paul gives that explanation to the Body.

t: What Does “Ye Are Gods” Mean in John 10:34 and Psalm 82:6?
s: Psalm 82 addresses Israel’s judges, who stand in God’s place and judge unjustly. Jesus quotes the line to answer a charge of blasphemy: if Scripture calls those who received God’s word “gods,” He whom the Father sanctified does not blaspheme in saying He is the Son of God. His claim rests on His works and His oneness with the Father.

t: Why Did Satan Quote Psalm 91 to Jesus? Matthew 4:6 & Psalm 91:11–12
s: Satan quotes Psalm 91 accurately but omits “in all thy ways,” turning a promise for the one who trusts God into a test of God. Jesus answers from Deuteronomy 6:16. The psalm is true; the use is false.

t: What Does “What Is Man” Mean in Psalm 8 and Hebrews 2?
s: Psalm 8 marvels at man’s place over God’s works. Hebrews reads the psalm in light of the world to come: the rule is not yet seen, but Jesus is seen, made lower and crowned. Hebrews applies the psalm to the Son of man and to Israel’s hope.

t: Should Believers Pray the Cursing Psalms? Psalm 69, Psalm 109, and Acts 1:20
s: Psalm 69 and 109 are David’s prayers against enemies. Acts 1 quotes Psalm 69:25 and 109:8 in Israel’s setting. The Body is not told to pray these psalms as its own. They are Scripture, but their setting is Israel’s.

t: Does “Be Ye Angry, and Sin Not” Permit Anger? Psalm 4:4 & Ephesians 4:26
s: Psalm 4:4 commands trembling and reflection. Paul quotes it to the Body and warns against sinning in anger. The psalm’s command is inward; Paul’s warning is practical.
a: Psalm 4:4 commands trembling and reflection. Paul quotes it to the Body and warns against sinning in anger. The psalm’s command is inward; Paul’s warning is practical.

t: Why Does Paul Say Christ “Gave Gifts” When Psalm 68 Says “Received”? Ephesians 4:8 & Psalm 68:18
s: Psalm 68 speaks of the victor receiving gifts. Paul applies the victory to Christ and states the result for the Body: He gave gifts. The psalm’s movement is upward; Paul’s application is downward.
a: Psalm 68 speaks of the victor receiving gifts. Paul applies the victory to Christ and states the result for the Body: He gave gifts. The psalm’s movement is upward; Paul’s application is downward.

t: Does “A Thousand Years Is as One Day” Explain the Delay? Psalm 90:4 & 2 Peter 3:8
s: Psalm 90 speaks of God’s eternity. Peter quotes it to answer scoffers and to show that delay does not deny promise. The psalm does not give a formula; Peter uses it to correct a charge.

t: What Is the “Rest” in Psalm 95 and Hebrews 3–4?
s: Psalm 95 warns Israel not to repeat the wilderness refusal. Hebrews applies the warning to Hebrew believers and speaks of a rest still open. The rest is Israel’s promised rest; the warning is present.
a: Psalm 95 warns Israel not to repeat the wilderness refusal. Hebrews applies the warning to Hebrew believers and speaks of a rest still open. The rest is Israel’s promised rest; the warning is present.

t: What Does “This Day Have I Begotten Thee” Mean? Psalm 2:7, Acts 13:33, and Hebrews 1:5
s: Psalm 2 speaks of the king God sets on Zion. Acts 13 applies the line to the resurrection; Hebrews applies it to sonship. The psalm’s line is used in two settings without merging them.
